chapter: Life on the road in the South
title: Deciding not to spend her life like this
summary: The incident made her decide she would not spend her life that way; she says Lake Charles itself had no such trouble.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: Did you have any other experiences like that?

Well, offhand, that was the one that really stood out in my mind all these many, many years, because it was a frightening experience. I personally don't think that they would have harmed me. I never did feel afraid for myself. I was afraid for this fellow, you know. But it was such a ridiculous thing to do to a person, you know, and knowing the type of guy this particular fellow was. And I thought about it, and I just couldn't -- and I got back home, and I'm glad that my dad wasn't along at the time, because it would have been a terrible scene with him, you know, because he would have been afraid, I'm sure, that they would have hurt me or something, and he was a very mild mannered man, but he didn't tolerate any foolishness. He didn't give it and he didn't take it, and he wasn't afraid of anybody and he had -- everybody had the greatest of respect for my dad, you know. So I was very happy that he wasn't there this particular time. So I began to think to myself, I didn't say anything to my parents or anything about it, but I began to think then and there, I says, 'Well, I am not going to spend the rest of my life like this.' And you know, we had never had any trouble in Lake Charles, not every, not any of my family or any of our friends, not with that type of thing, you know, because we all got along
very well there in that little town, and --
Was that sort of thing more apt to happen in Texas?
Well, at that time I would say so, yes. At that particular --
I've heard a few other stories from musicians about Texas and guns and usually Texans who have been drinking and then make demands with their guns.
